mainTopic: A seller's bias when testifying about a field he sold שלא באחריות, a seller's responsibility when a גוי seizes a sold donkey, and רבה's limit on the rule that a craftsman has no חזקה.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier ruling: a person who sold a field without a guarantee (שלא באחריות) may not testify that the field belongs to the buyer, because he wants it kept available for his own creditor. The גמרא asks what he gains either way. If he has other land, the creditor collects from that. If he has none, it makes no difference to him. The answer is that he does not want to be a לוה רשע ולא ישלם, a wicked borrower who never pays. He does not feel the same way toward the buyer, because he can say: that is why I sold it to you without a guarantee. Next, רבא (or רב פפא) publicly announced that if a Jew sells a donkey and a גוי seizes it, the seller must rescue it. This applies unless the buyer recognizes the animal as born to the seller's donkey, or the גוי took the saddle too. אמימר says the seller is never responsible, because an ordinary גוי is presumed to be a robber. Finally, the גמרא returns to the rule that an אומן has no חזקה. רבה limits it to a case where witnesses saw the item handed over, since without witnesses the craftsman could have denied ever receiving it. אביי objects that even with witnesses he could say 'I returned it,' and רבה's reply begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next.

steps.title: What Does the Seller Gain Either Way?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that the seller is biased. Either he has other land, so his creditor collects from that, or he has none, so the outcome does not affect him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he has other land, the creditor will go collect from that land! If he has no other land, what difference does it make to him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason given for disqualifying the seller as a witness. It sets up two possibilities and argues that in neither one does the seller have anything to gain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier reason was that the seller wants the sold field kept available for his creditor. If the seller owns other land, the creditor can simply collect from it, so the sold field does not matter to the seller. If the seller owns nothing else, the creditor can never collect from him anyway, so again he has no stake.

keyTerms.meaning: Other land (land the seller still owns)
Goes back to (the creditor turns to collect from it)
What difference does it make to him?

phrases.english: If he has other land,
phrases.notes: "He" is the seller who wants to testify about the field he sold.

phrases.english: the creditor will go after that land of his!
If he does not have other land,
what difference does it make to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given before this point for disqualifying the seller's testimony.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the seller is biased because he wants the field kept for his creditor.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both possibilities, having other land or having none, leave the seller with nothing to gain from his testimony.

steps.title: He Does Not Want to Be a Borrower Who Never Pays
steps.stepSummary: The case really is one where the seller has no other land. He still wants his debt paid so he will not be a לוה רשע ולא ישלם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is a case where he has no other land. He says to himself: I am not comfortable being 'the wicked one who borrows and does not pay.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by choosing the second possibility: the seller has no other land. His bias is not about money. It is about his reputation and his conscience.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though no one can force him to pay, the seller wants his debt paid off somehow. If the sold field stays with the buyer, the creditor can collect it from there. That gives the seller a personal reason to testify that the field belongs to the buyer, so his testimony is biased.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (the גמרא keeps one side of the challenge)
It is not comfortable or pleasing to him
The wicked borrows and does not pay (תהלים 37:21)

steps.confusionAlert: The seller is not trying to avoid a legal payment here. He has nothing to be taken from. His concern is about not being seen as, or being, someone who leaves a debt unpaid.

phrases.english: Actually, it is where he does not have other land,
because he says: It is not comfortable for me
to be 'the wicked borrows and does not pay.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 1 by choosing its second possibility.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a non-financial motive for the bias.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With no other land, the seller has no stake in the outcome.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller cares about his debt being paid so he will not be a לוה רשע ולא ישלם.

steps.title: He Is Also Failing to Pay the Buyer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if the field is taken from the buyer, the seller is also a borrower who does not pay toward the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, toward the other person as well, he is 'the wicked borrows and does not pay'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 2. If the seller is so worried about not paying debts, he should be just as worried about the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer paid the seller for the field. If the creditor then takes the field, the buyer is left with nothing for his money. So either way the seller fails to pay someone back, and that seems to cancel out his supposed motive.

keyTerms.meaning: In the end, ultimately
The other one (here, the buyer)

phrases.english: Ultimately, with regard to the other one as well,
phrases.notes: "The other one" is the buyer, who paid for a field that the creditor then takes.

phrases.english: he is 'the wicked borrows and does not pay'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The motive of not wanting to be a לוה רשע ולא ישלם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same motive should apply toward the buyer, so it cannot explain why the seller favors the creditor.

steps.title: The Buyer Accepted the Risk
steps.stepSummary: The seller can tell the buyer: this is exactly why I sold it to you without a guarantee.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say: That is why I sold it to you without a guarantee.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the seller owes the buyer nothing. The buyer knowingly bought without אחריות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the sale was made שלא באחריות, the buyer accepted the risk that the field might be taken from him. So the seller is not a borrower who fails to pay toward the buyer. His only real debt is to the creditor, and that keeps him biased.

keyTerms.meaning: I sold
Without a guarantee (the seller does not promise to pay back the buyer if the field is taken)

steps.whatToRemember: The seller of a field שלא באחריות cannot testify for the buyer. He wants the field kept available so his creditor gets paid and he avoids being a לוה רשע ולא ישלם. He owes the buyer nothing, because the buyer accepted the risk.

phrases.english: Because he says: For this reason I sold it to you
without a guarantee.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר: לְהָכִי זַבֵּינִי לָךְ שֶׁלֹּא בְּאַחְרָיוּת
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes between the two parties: the seller has a debt to the creditor but none to the buyer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The seller fails both the creditor and the buyer equally.
steps.terutzMaskana: The buyer accepted the risk by buying שלא באחריות, so the seller owes him nothing.

steps.title: Public Announcement: The Seller Must Rescue a Seized Donkey
steps.stepSummary: רבא (or רב פפא) announced to all travelers: if a Jew sold a donkey and a גוי seized it from the buyer, the seller must rescue it from the גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא announced, and some say it was רב פפא: Those who go up and those who go down should know: if a Jew sold a donkey to another Jew, and a גוי came and seized it from him, the law is that the seller must rescue it from him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. A public announcement makes a ruling known to everyone traveling between בבל and ארץ ישראל: the seller is responsible when a גוי seizes an animal he sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גוי claims the donkey was really his. The ruling puts the burden on the seller, not the buyer, to get the donkey back or make up the loss. Because it was announced publicly, it was meant to be widely known and practiced.

keyTerms.meaning: Announced publicly
Some say (another version of who said it)
Those who go up and those who go down (travelers between בבל and ארץ ישראל)
Seizes by force
Rescues or recovers it

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling opens a new discussion about when a seller is responsible for an item that is taken from the buyer after the sale.

phrases.english: Rava announced, and some say it was Rav Pappa:
Those who go up and those who go down should know;
phrases.notes: Literally "those who go up above and those who go down below": people traveling between בבל and ארץ ישראל.

phrases.aramaic: הַאי בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּזָבֵין לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא
phrases.english: this Jew who sold a donkey
to his fellow Jew,

phrases.aramaic: וְקָא אָתֵי גּוֹי וְאָנֵיס לֵיהּ מִינֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: and a gentile came and seized it from him,
phrases.notes: The גוי claims the donkey was really his, and "him" is the buyer.

phrases.english: the law is that he must rescue it from him.
phrases.notes: "He" is the seller, who must get the donkey back from the גוי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the testimony discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a גוי seizes a donkey from the Jew who bought it, the Jewish seller must rescue it or make good the loss.

steps.title: Two limits on the seller's duty to rescue the donkey
steps.stepSummary: The seller's duty applies only when the buyer cannot recognize the animal as the offspring of the seller's donkey, and only when the גוי did not seize the saddle as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when the buyer does not recognize the animal as the offspring of the seller's donkey. If he does recognize it, the seller is not responsible. And we only said this when the גוי did not seize the animal together with its saddle. If he seized it with the saddle, the seller is not responsible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the ruling from step 5. It gives two cases where the seller does NOT have to step in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller is responsible only when the גוי's claim might be true, meaning the donkey might really have been stolen from him. If the buyer knows the animal was born to the seller's own donkey, the גוי is obviously lying, so the loss is simple robbery and not the seller's fault. Grabbing the saddle too shows the same thing, because the גוי had no claim to the saddle at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And we only said this when… (a phrase that limits a ruling)
Recognizes, knows
The offspring of his (the seller's) donkey
Seized by force
Saddle

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַכִּיר בָּהּ
phrases.english: And we only said this where he does not recognize it
phrases.notes: 'He' is the buyer, and 'it' is the donkey the גוי grabbed.

phrases.english: that it is the offspring of his donkey,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מַכִּיר בָּהּ שֶׁהִיא בַּת חֲמוֹרוֹ – לָא.
phrases.english: but if he recognizes that it is the offspring of his donkey, no.
phrases.notes: 'No' means the seller does not have to step in. The גוי is clearly just a robber.

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא אָנֵיס לֵיהּ
phrases.english: And we only said this where he did not seize it
together with the saddle,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אָנֵיס לֵיהּ לְדִידֵיהּ וּלְאוּכָּפָא – לָא.
phrases.english: but if he seized it together with the saddle, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling of step 5 by naming two cases where it does not apply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seller must rescue the donkey only when the גוי's claim might be true. If the buyer recognizes the animal as the seller's donkey's offspring, or the גוי also took the saddle, the seller is not responsible.

steps.title: אמימר: the seller is never responsible
steps.stepSummary: אמימר says that even without these signs the seller is not responsible, because an ordinary גוי is presumed to be a robber. He supports this with a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: even if none of these signs are present, the seller is not responsible. Why? It is well known that an ordinary גוי takes things by force, as the פסוק says: 'Whose mouth speaks falsehood, and their right hand is a right hand of lying.'
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר disagrees with the ruling and its limits. He says the seller never has to step in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two limits in step 6 freed the seller only when there was clear proof the גוי was lying. אמימר says no proof is needed, because we always assume an ordinary גוי's seizure is plain robbery. That means the seller sold a good animal, and the loss is not his responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: None of these (signs) are present
What is the reason?
An ordinary, typical גוי
One who takes things by force; a robber

steps.whyThisMatters: אמימר's view removes the seller's responsibility completely. It reverses the practical result of רבא's announcement in step 5.

phrases.aramaic: אַמֵּימָר אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ לֵיכָּא כׇּל הָנֵי – לָא.
phrases.english: Ameimar said: even if none of these are present, no.
phrases.notes: 'These' are the two signs from the last step. 'No' means the seller is still not responsible.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

phrases.aramaic: מִידָּע יָדַע דִּסְתַם גּוֹי אַנָּס הוּא –
phrases.english: It is well known that an ordinary gentile is one who seizes by force,
as it is stated: "Whose mouth speaks falsehood,
and their right hand is a right hand of lying."

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ לֵיכָּא כׇּל הָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with steps 5 and 6. It frees the seller in every case, not only in the two special ones.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seller is never responsible when a גוי seizes the animal, because an ordinary גוי is presumed to be a robber.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two views. The first makes the seller step in unless clear signs show the גוי is lying. אמימר says the seller is never responsible, because a גוי's seizure is always presumed to be robbery.

steps.title: רבה: a craftsman lacks חזקה only when witnesses saw the handover
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the rule that an אומן has no חזקה. רבה limits it to a case where the item was given to him in front of witnesses. Without witnesses, the craftsman could have denied ever receiving it, so his claim that he bought it is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A craftsman has no חזקה,' and so on. רבה said: this was taught only when the owner gave him the item in front of witnesses. But if he gave it without witnesses, the craftsman could have said, 'This never happened.' So when he says instead, 'I bought it,' he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the donkey case and goes back to an earlier rule about craftsmen. רבה adds a limit to that rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a craftsman holding an item cannot claim he bought it, since items are handed to him to work on. רבה says this applies only when witnesses saw the handover. With no witnesses, the craftsman could have kept the item by claiming it was always his. So we believe his weaker-sounding claim, 'I bought it,' through a מיגו (since he could have made a better claim).

keyTerms.meaning: A craftsman who receives items to work on
A presumption of ownership based on possession
Since he could have said… (the logic of מיגו)
These things never happened (a full denial)
I bought it, and that is why it is in my hand
He is believed

phrases.english: A craftsman does not have a presumption of ownership, etc.
Rabba said: they taught this only
where he handed it to him in front of witnesses,
but if he handed it to him without witnesses,
since he could say to him
"These things never happened,"
phrases.notes: He means: you never gave me anything, this item was always mine.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אָמַר לֵיהּ נָמֵי ״לְקוּחָה הִיא בְּיָדִי״ –
phrases.english: when he says to him instead "It is purchased and in my hand,"
he is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁמָּסַר לוֹ בְּעֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to the earlier rule about craftsmen.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A craftsman cannot claim he bought the item only when witnesses saw it handed to him. Without witnesses, a מיגו makes his claim believable.
steps.confusionAlert: רבה is not saying a craftsman is a kind of owner. He still has no חזקה from holding the item. He is believed here only because of what he could have claimed instead.

steps.title: אביי: even with witnesses the craftsman should be believed
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבה. Even with witnesses, the craftsman could claim 'I returned it to you,' so by the same logic his claim that he bought it should be believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: if so, even when there were witnesses he should be believed! He could have said, 'I returned it to you,' so when he says, 'I bought it,' he should be believed.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's reasoning. He shows that the same 'he could have said something better' logic also works when there are witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses prove the item was handed over, but they do not prove it was never given back. So even with witnesses, the craftsman could have said 'I returned it' and been free of payment. By רבה's own logic, his claim that he bought it should also be believed, and then the rule that a craftsman has no חזקה would almost never apply.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introducing a problem with what was just said)
In front of witnesses
I returned it to you

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: if so,
even with witnesses as well,
since he could say to him: "I returned it to you,"
when he says to him: "It is purchased and in my hand,"
he should be believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's reasoning from step 8 directly.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's limit that a craftsman is believed only when no witnesses saw the handover
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Witnesses do not rule out the claim 'I returned it.' So the same מיגו applies even with witnesses, and רבה's line between witnesses and no witnesses falls apart.

steps.title: רבה begins answering אביי
steps.stepSummary: רבה opens his reply to אביי with the words 'Do you think that...', getting ready to show that אביי's challenge rests on a mistaken assumption.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to אביי: Do you think that...
steps.whatsHappening: רבה is starting his answer to אביי's challenge from Step 9. This line only sets up his answer, and the real content comes in the next piece.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'מִי סָבְרַתְּ' (do you think that...?) is a common way to begin an answer. The speaker points to an idea the questioner assumed and suggests that it is not correct. Here רבה is getting ready to show why the 'I returned it' argument does not work once there are witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: "Do you think that...?" An opening that questions an assumption the other person made.
"He said to him." It introduces a direct reply to the person who just spoke.

steps.confusionAlert: Even though 'מִי סָבְרַתְּ' sounds like a question, רבה is not asking for information. He is beginning his answer by challenging אביי's assumption.

phrases.english: Rabbah said to him:
Do you think that...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is רבה's reply to אביי's קשיא in Step 9. It opens his defense of the ruling he gave in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting an assumption (this is only the opening; the full answer comes next).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי assumed that, even with witnesses, the אומן could believably say 'I returned it,' so his claim 'I bought it' should be believed as well.
steps.terutzMaskana: Not yet stated. רבה is about to show that אביי's assumption is wrong.
